lessons.md:
- Scaling = 3 elements: **Functions** (what the business must do: product, marketing, sales, CS, IT, recruiting, HR, finance), **People** (who does them), **Operations** (glue: meetings, comms, training).
- Stages are organized by **headcount**, not revenue: a 35-person restaurant ($2M) and a 35-person software company ($100M) organize the same way. Revenue depends on the opportunity; structure depends on headcount.
- Each stage = one-word theme, headcount, founder role, leadership layers, # of US companies there, the constraint + "graduate" action for each of the 8 functions, and one **bottom line** objective.
- Guidelines, not laws. Being ahead in one function = it's probably not your constraint; skipping steps = future weak link.
- **Only study your stage, the one before and the one after.** "Companies die of indigestion, not starvation." Strategy = putting limited resources on the constraint.

| # | Stage | Headcount | Founder role | Bottom line / how you graduate   |
| 0 | Improvise | 0 | Researcher | Nothing is happening → get people to try your stuff **for free** |
| 1 | Monetize | 1 | Starter | No money → make your **first sale** |
| 2 | Advertise | 1 (+freelancers) | Doer | New customers inconsistent → **Rule of 100** daily advertising |
| 3 | Stabilize | 1–4 | Trainer | Too much for one person → **get help** (first hires) |
| 4 | Prioritize | 5–9 | Manager | Trying to be everything to everyone → **niche down** to best customer |
| 5 | Productize | 10–19 | Director | Low LTV:CAC → build a **second (premium) product** |
| 6 | Optimize | 20–49 | Leader | Everything inefficient → grow by doing things **better, not more** |
| 7 | Categorize | 50–99 | Executive | Systems overwhelmed → **triage & organize**; add 2nd acquisition channel |
| 8 | Specialize | 100–249 | President | No one can know everything → **dedicated people/teams** per task |
| 9 | Capitalize | 250–500 | Chairman | Unsure where next growth comes from → **make a big bet** (M&A or R&D) |

Key per-stage graduations (early stages, most relevant to a solo founder): - **Improvise**: make something free; tell people about it; get people to try it free; service free customers; get basic tech; recruit yourself (increase work capacity); create an entity; open business bank account. - **Monetize**: fix product until V1 good enough to sell; tell people about paid stuff + use free ad credits; use results from free users to sell paid ones ("offer to solve their problem for money"); talk to free users to find hidden costs (why they don't use/like it); free tools; friends/family/freelancers for skill gaps; basic vendor agreements; set up payment processor → first deposit. - **Advertise**: fix product "in an unscalable way" (jump over the moon); **Rule of 100** (100 dials / 100 min content / 100 of anything daily); nail a setting + closing script (CLOSER framework); learn to handle angry customers + collect testimonials (Epiphany Bridge); free trials of tech; convert part-timers to full-timers; bookkeeping, save taxes quarterly, check bank daily ("what gets measured gets managed"). - **Stabilize**: fix the ONE thing customers complain most about; add long-term nurture (email/content) for colder audiences; set basic qualifications + outsource setting/calendaring; consistent onboarding; cut unused tools; basic sales pipeline (even on paper); write job descriptions; payroll provider; basic bookkeeping/invoices. - **Prioritize**: specialize product (V2) for a niche avatar — "go deep, not wide"; better free stuff + qualification friction (don't open a 2nd channel yet); track KPIs on a spreadsheet: contact rate, schedule rate, show rate, offer rate, close rate, cash collected; CS KPIs + CRM notes; shared tools (project mgmt, Slack, password manager); proper interviews + reference checks; employee handbook; P&L, cash-flow statement, insurance. - **Productize**: connect CS to product to find what else customers want → 2nd product; lead scoring, attribution, CRO; sales aids (VSLs, webinars), weekly "game tape" across sales/CS/marketing, NPS/CSAT/refund rate by rep; CS playbook + ascension path; company-owned hardware; promote deliberately (avoid Peter Principle), pay employee referrals = your cost to acquire talent; termination policy; budget + forecast. - Later stages: product improvement pipelines with owners, ad assembly process, sales training systems, churn by cohort, cybersecurity/offboarding, headhunting, benefits (Optimize); feature teams, 2nd channel funded by referrals + segmented nurture, ATS, HRIS, department budgets (Categorize); prune product (improve by deletion), brand + standard messaging, route best leads to best closers, specialized tech stacks, founder fit-check, audits, renegotiate everything (Specialize); M&A/R&D, brand-first omnichannel, specialized sales/CS by product/territory, founder recruits stars personally, workforce planning, prep-for-sale/QoE (Capitalize). - Stats: only 9% of people start a business; only 24% of businesses have an employee; ~3M US companies have 5–9 people; ~1.2M have 50–99; ~300k reach 250–500.

lessons.t: Scaling 3 — Improvise (stage 0, just you, role = researcher; 32 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: nothing is happening → get people to try your stuff for FREE.**

Objective is to learn more than earn.

# Product
Give something away free. Pick a mechanism (software / media / service / physical).
Free thing should either (a) **reveal a problem** (assessment, e.g. chiropractor posture scan), (b) be a **free trial** of a solution they need ongoing (speed-test fix for 7 days), or (c) be **one step of a multi-step process** (first coat of garage sealant).
Things people sell: services, products, access, risk, money, media, data, software. B2C services = things people know how to do but hate doing; B2B services = doing a function (product, IT, marketing…) better/faster than the business can — "fractional expert".
Start with unscalable 1-on-1 value, fronted at your own cost, to get feedback.

# Marketing — the Core Four
(the only 4 ways to tell people): **warm outreach, cold outreach, post free content, run paid ads.** Start with **warm outreach** (cheapest, fastest): every contact you've ever had, every follower — 100 people who know you beat 100 cold leads. Both Alex and Leila started personal training by posting free offers on Facebook.
"If you have no money you should have no shame — knock, call, email, text, DM, ask." Posting content is often used as an excuse to avoid rejection. Choose: fear of judgment, or fear of never having a business.

# Sales
Just get them to try it free. Ask their problems; offer to solve them in exchange for **the 4 R's: Review, Referral, Retention (later pay), Resale/ascension**.
Objective: discover **perceived hidden costs** (things they must start doing, stop doing, risks, effort, time delay). Remove everything that sucks and you can charge nearly infinite (the "click a button get a six-pack" thought experiment).

# Customer service
Service free customers like they pay you — always available, fast, no job too small, no resentment. Your only edge vs better products is **ruthless execution**.
Remove the word "scale" from your mind. McKinsey: more customers leave due to bad service than product/price (T-Mobile won share purely on service).

# IT
Tech only needs to (1) let you communicate with people and (2) deliver your stuff.

# Recruiting
Recruit yourself — build work capacity. 5am–11pm for 6–12 months if needed (Alex & Leila slept in extended stays, 4am–11pm).
Hormozi quotes: beat 99% by preparing the night before, showing up early, leaving when the job's done right, remembering names, following up, improving one thing at a time. "Work exceptionally hard, get rejected, live below your means for 3 years and you beat almost everyone." "Find what works → do more → find what's preventing more → solve → repeat." "Good enough at almost anything in 20 focused hours; most people spend a decade delaying the first hour." 10 hours testing > 10 years reading.

# HR
Form an entity (LLC/S-corp) to separate personal from business assets.

# Finance
Business bank account; run all work expenses through it (phone, computer, internet, home office portion) to write them off. Banks pay sign-up bonuses ($300–400).
The average small business costs ~$3,500 to start.

> **Bottom line: business makes no money → make your first paid sale.**

Then you're one of ~30M US companies (top ~9% of people).

# Product
Fix it until it's good enough to sell (V1) by finding the **hidden costs**: ask "Why won't you pay? What makes this a no? What would make it a yes? **What would it take?**" **Magic question**: "If I asked $3,000 for 3 months to get you [goal], what would it need to look like for you to be excited to move forward?" — they design it with price already set; work backwards.
Don't decide what you're unwilling to do divorced of price (would you pick them up for $1,000/session? probably). Hence charge a premium to afford a different, more valuable service.
Don't refuse to get 10 clients because of problems at 10 — get them first.

> **Value Equation** = (Dream Outcome × Perceived Likelihood of Achievement) ÷ (Time Delay × Effort & Sacrifice).
Xanax vs meditation example. Shorthand: **good, fast, risk-free, easy.**

# Marketing — Proof > Promise
Alex never sells until he has **10+ testimonials** (easier to sell + gives him conviction).
The proof continuum (stronger → weaker):
- In-person > virtual
- Live > recorded
- **raw > processed** (iPhone selfies convert better)
- Show > tell
- Others say it > you say it
- **identical to prospect** > different (Gym Launch: matching testimonial demographics to the market lifted conversion)
- Specific/personal > generic
- Big + small results > bad/no results
- **new > old** (people assume your last testimonial was your last good result)
- Lots > few ("overwhelming social proof" — floor-to-ceiling framed reviews)
- Numbers > no numbers
- Track record > none

Ad platforms give $50–500 free credits.

# Sales
Use free results to sell paid. Script idea (from $100M Leads), paraphrased: you're only taking a handful of people so each gets real attention; they get it at a steep discount (e.g. 80% off) in exchange for actually using it, giving feedback and leaving a review if it earns one — then ask if that sounds fair. **Raise price 20% every 5 sales**: free → 80% off → 60% → 40% → 20% → full → keep going.
Gym Launch went $6k → 8 → 10 → 12 → 16 → 20 → 22 → 30 → 35 → 50k. If nobody buys: do you have proof for the claim, are you actually asking, with conviction?

# Customer service
Talk to free users; sort problems into **result issues** vs **experience issues**. People stay more for good experience + bad result than bad experience + good result.
Fix results: set expectations in the sale, match goals, define workflow/milestones. Fix experience: easier, faster, more pleasant.

# Recruiting
Friends + freelancers (Upwork, Fiverr, 99designs) for skill/time gaps, no fixed cost — your needs change too fast to hire right now.

# HR — vendor agreement test
Who's involved, who does what, where, by when, how much, for how long, who says it's good, what happens if it isn't. Agreements clarify more than they protect.
You must decide what you want — don't wait for a vendor to create a unicorn.

# Finance
At least 2 ways to get paid (cash + card processor: Stripe, bank, Skool, Shopify); graduate when a payment lands in the business bank account.

lessons.t: Scaling 5 — Advertise (stage 2, still just you + freelancers, role = DOER; 33 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: new customers are inconsistent → let more people know about your stuff, every single day.**

Biggest mistake: copying what Alex/Leila do now instead of being in the weeds.

# Product — valuable over scalable
Paying customers have higher expectations. Do more work by hand so they get the result, then build the scalable version.
(ACQ's addiction treatment center pays flights + airport pickup — every benefit has a cost; if they'll pay and you'll deliver, that's free exchange.) New founders spend so long making offers scalable they forget to make them valuable.

# Marketing — Rule of 100, daily
100 dials / outreaches / texts / emails every day, not when you need clients. Biggest error: stopping advertising once you have enough customers.
Excess demand = good problem.

- Core Four applied: **warm** (people who know you), **cold** (LinkedIn filters, friends-of-friends, bought lists) — private 1:1; **content** = 100 min/day: make the post, DM everyone who liked/commented, then leave 50–100 best-in-thread comments on others' posts aimed at your audience (you only compete with the other commenters); **paid ads** = $10–100/day and 100 minutes on hooks/creative.

# Sales — nail a script for setting + closing
78% of businesses sell 1:1. **CLOSER framework**:

**C**larify why they're here ("What made you opt in / reply?")

**L**abel them with a problem ("So you want to get from X to Y, right?")

**O**verview past pain: "What have you tried? How'd that work? What did you like/not like? What else?" — exhaust every past attempt. Motivation = deprivation; remind them how hungry they are.

**S**ell the vacation, not the plane flight — **3-pillar pitch**: 3 things needed for success, each with a one-liner + analogy (fitness / nutrition / accountability = three legs of a stool; "brushing teeth" analogy for accountability). Pitch = 2–3 minutes; most of the call is about them.

**E**xplain away concerns: **time, stall, money, preference, authority** (decision maker).

**R**einforce the decision (great onboarding).

- Two-step sale: the **setter does C-L-O only** — get them "starving", then "you'd be a good fit, let me set you up with John". During calls use **AAA**: **Acknowledge** ("so I'm hearing X, is that right?"), **Associate** ("that's just like our best customers"), **Ask** the next question — keeps it non-robotic.

# Customer service
Paid customers complain more.

# Angry boat
Only one person fits in the angry boat — get MORE upset than them on their behalf and they back off.

# HEAR framework
**H**ear them out (let them vent, shut up, short acknowledgments) → **E**mpathize/acknowledge and escalate beyond their upset → **A**pologize (take accountability) → **R**esolve with them: offer ~3 options ("I could refund you, but I know you want this; I can get you into the next date; or I'll upgrade you to the next level on us — which sounds best, or did I miss something?").
Never cower from an upset customer.

# Epiphany Bridge testimonial script
Internal struggle (rock bottom feelings) → external struggle (objective metrics before) → **skepticism** ("what were your concerns before joining?" — prospects relate to the pain more than the solution) → why did you do it anyway / why us, why then → external victory (metrics now) → internal victory (best moment, what can you do now that you couldn't, what pain is gone).
Customer service is always a resell.

# IT
Free tech + trials: lead-capture site, starter CRM, basic automation (auto-replies, appointment text reminders). Early Gym Launch: thank-you page with Leila's photo + "text Leila two times that work for you".

# Recruiting
Too much work for part-timers/freelancers → convert part-timers to full-time ("you said you don't like your job — come work for me" = make them an offer); post on social ("I'm looking for X, here's what it's like, apply here") + Indeed/LinkedIn. Alex's EA Yasmee came from a Facebook post and has followed him through 4 companies.

# HR
Don't treat contractors as employees (IRS 20-point test; ~5 yeses = employee) — back taxes + penalties risk compounds with headcount and time. Everything in business is managing risk, not eliminating it.

# Finance
QuickBooks-equivalent; a non-sketchy CPA; save & pay taxes **quarterly**; **check your bank account daily** (like weighing yourself daily — fast feedback beats precise feedback at this stage).

lessons.t: Scaling 6 — Stabilize (stage 3, 1–4 employees, role = TRAINER; 33 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: workload exceeds your resources → get help.**

Only ~24% of businesses have even one employee — you're further ahead than you think. The first few hires set the culture.

# Product
Volume creates cracks → fix the thing they **complain about most** / that creates the highest **activation**. Prioritize fixes by ROI: size of effect × likelihood it works ÷ investment.
Shortcut: what's the #1 reason they cancel/leave? Fix that.

> **Activation** = the point the customer first receives value.
Track both outcomes (Gym Launch: a sale in week 1 from the leads) and behaviors that lead to it (attended first coach call).

# Impact vs investment matrix
(RICE:
- Reach, impact, confidence, expense): high-impact/low-cost = do first (usually already done)
- Low/low = "golden BBs" (delegate later)
- High/high = where real growth is — "big hairy problems" touching 2–3 departments

Entrepreneurs hide in B-minus/C-plus quick wins for months. **Put a money tag on the big problem** ("cut churn in half = $20M") to stay motivated.
With few resources: **fewer, bigger wins.**

# Marketing
Leads are colder than your first warm prospects → add **long-term nurture** (email and/or content) to expand your warm pool.

- Email cadence: minimum 1 blast/week to whole list; ideal 3×/week segmented. Structure (Mozi Money Minute): **subject → quick hit of value (e.g. quote) → tactical value → light CTA ("by the way, if you want help…") → PS that trains the click** (meme/reward). Example value: belief-breaking formula — state wrong belief, why it's wrong, what's right, proof.
- Content = nurture more than lead gen. Every piece: **Hook → Retain (value) → Reward.** Topics: far-past stories, recent past (check last week's calendar/customer issues), present (what's top of mind — capture ideas e.g. tweets), trending, manufactured ("I lived on $100/month for 2 years"). Formats: **lists, steps, stories** (interweave).

# Sales
Wasting time on bad leads → decide basic **qualifications** (who will we NOT sell — usually your worst, loudest, most time-consuming customers) + outsource setting/calendaring. Gym Launch qualifiers: small fitness gym, ≥3 employees, ≥30 clients (needed for the paid-in-full play), not yoga/barre/personal trainer. **BANT** (IBM): Budget, Authority, Need, Timing.
B2B outbound voicemail trick: "Hey, this is John calling in regards to [competitor across the street], call me back" → instant callbacks.

# Customer service — GROWTH onboarding
**G**oal-setting/expectations → **R**esource/time allocation (personal success path) → **O**ptimize first experience (quick wins, get to activation fast) → **W**orkflow integration (fit their life, add nothing new) → **T**rack & feedback loops (monitor, recognize, reward; **"book a meeting from a meeting"**) → **H**and off to ongoing support (make sure they know exactly where to ask questions).

# IT
Cut unused tools; build a basic **sales pipeline** you track: opt-ins → scheduled → showed → offered → closed → cash collected (with a metric for each). "You cannot improve without knowing where you are."

# Recruiting
Write job descriptions **like ads** — hook/headline (dream job, why here not across the street) → retain (values & how they show up in the role) → educate (top 3 responsibilities, impact) → reinforce (pay, benefits, perks, awards). Leila rewriting headlines took companies from 10 applicants/week to 30/day.
Resume review: past achievements with objective data, relevant experience, transferable skills; reject irrelevant/too much/too little. **Target 20% pass-rate to screening call.** Beware overqualified "stage-7 habits" in a stage-3 company — hire for now + next 12–18 months.

# HR
Payroll provider (Gusto for small; ADP/Paychex big) handles taxes per state, esp. remote teams.

# Finance
Billing process (contracts entered right), **collections** (few roles pay for themselves faster), set aside fixed/recurring bills first, a single inbox (ap@/finance@) for incoming bills; AR/AP.

lessons.t: Scaling 7 — Prioritize (stage 4, 5–9 employees, role = MANAGER; 43 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: you're trying to be everything to everyone → niche down to serve only people like your best customers.**

~3M US companies here. In revenue terms this usually bites around $1–3M ("one of the five horsemen" where businesses stall).

# Product → V2 for a niche avatar
Run an **80/20 on customers**: which 20% pay the most, complain least, love you most, cost least to fulfil? Build and price the product for them. Workshop example: a B2B lead-gen agency wanted plastic surgeons (because he had more of them), but **law firms** had ~2× LTV, barely used support and gave better reviews.
"Who are your law firms?"

- Why niching wins: one message → easier to attract; one prospect type → easier to train sales; templated delivery → better margins. Replace the bottom 80% with more of the top 20% and revenue can triple on the same infrastructure. "Generalize before you specialize." Don't become "the CRM of your industry" (e.g. a marketing agency deciding to also close its clients' leads).

# Niche pricing
Time management $19 → for sales pros $99 → for B2B outbound sales pros $1,000 → for outbound reps selling power tools $10,000. Same core deliverable; value rises with who it's for.
Price to the customer you deliver the most value to, not the weakest one.

# Marketing
Too many unqualified leads → **better free stuff** (spend real hard cost on lead magnets competitors can't afford — if 4× leads lowers CAC, you net a gain), **more creative volume** (old content/ad spend fatigues), and **qualification/friction** so volume self-selects (give the great free thing only to people who qualify).
Match messaging click-to-close to the new avatar (ads, lead magnet, offer, funnel, application questions, scripts, nurture); make the call-out specific ("attorneys with 5+ full-time lawyers").

# Sales
Speed-to-contact drops + no metrics → track KPIs in Google Sheets: contact rate, schedule rate, cancellation rate, **show rate**, offer rate, close rate, cash collected — per rep; advanced: scheduled-call-to-close %, opt-in-to-close %.

- Show-rate playbook: thank-you page headline sells booking the call (truthful scarcity/urgency); **scheduler above the fold** + multiple booking prompts; **15-minute slots, 7 days/week, 9am–9pm** (ALAN data: availability was the #1 correlate of sales); stack people for coverage; pay **setters ~3% of closed sales**; automated reminders (clearly labelled automated) **plus** manual ones (morning-of / 24h and 1h before) — human-sent reminders roughly doubled show-up vs AI-customised automation; **public kudos for leading indicators** (show rate, follow-up, following the script) — people work harder for status than money; **show-up bribe** (gift card, $500 credit toward first month, a t-shirt set aside in their size).
- Insight: going from 50% → 80% show rate lifts revenue more than a 35% → 42% close-rate gain, and it's process, not skill.
- Portfolio story: a 14-location medical business — they did just ONE thing first: **tripled price** (LTV 4×) by specializing product + messaging to the right avatar, then fixed the upsell script (recurring revenue 10×). "Growth is decided by the quality of your prioritization."

# Customer service
Install KPIs — **NPS** (0–10 "how likely to recommend":
- 9–10 promoters, 7–8 neutral, ≤6 detractors
- Range −100…+100
- Average company ≈ −12, Apple ≈ 61, Chick-fil-A ≈ 58, ACQ workshops 91), **CSAT** (5-point, asked right after a specific touchpoint), churn %, **revenue churn**, refund/chargeback %

Aim for **net negative churn** (expansion revenue from top customers outweighs losses). **Centralize notes per customer** so the company has "one brain" — 5 min of note review before a call makes you look elite.
Also log complaints/friction centrally. Data depth: shallow (NPS/CSAT/CES) → medium (open surveys) → deep (interviews, focus groups).

# IT
Move off texts → Slack; password manager (LastPass — instantly revoke access); shared project management (Asana/Monday/ClickUp) — only works if everyone uses it.

# Recruiting
**two-step interview**: (1) short screen for **expectations** (pay, location, hours) → (2) interview for **culture/values fit, skill fit (top 3–5 skills), potential fit** → select + **check references** properly (you'd research a $7k/month software for hours; do the same for a $7k/month hire — people have more practice lying than you have detecting lies).

# HR
Employee handbook — welcome/mission/values, employment policies, code of conduct, schedules/remote, comp, benefits, leave, performance, safety, anti-discrimination, tech use, resignation/termination, signed acknowledgement.

# Finance
P&L (did we make money) + **cash-flow statement** (can we survive till tomorrow — you can be profitable and cash-negative); general liability insurance; plan for "lumpy" one-off purchases.

lessons.t: Scaling 8 — Productize (stage 5, 10–19 employees, role = DIRECTOR; 60 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: LTV:CAC too low because customers have nothing else to buy → make and sell a second, premium product.**

~2.4M US companies here (often ~$3–10M revenue).

# Product — the back-end upsell
Customers are fractal: inside your best 20% there's another 20% who'll spend ~5×. Rule of thumb: back-end ≈ **5× the core offer price**.
Math: 100 buyers × $1k = $100k; if 20 of them buy a $5k back-end → another $100k = revenue doubled, LTV:CAC roughly doubled. Easiest upsells: **more of the thing → more help with it → a better/newer version → for longer.** Let CS + sales tell you which one customers ask for.

# The "Crazy 8"
8 ways to make any customer more valuable: (1) raise price, (2) get them to buy again more often (or reduce churn), (3) lower your cost to deliver, (4) cross-sell a complementary thing, (5) upsell quality, (6) upsell quantity, (7) downsell quality, (8) downsell quantity (downsells turn a "no" into some money — revenue per lead).

- Agency example (relevant to Egor): raise fees; reduce churn; offshore delivery or raise client:rep ratio (1 rep serves 10 instead of 5); cross-sell SEO/creative/email on top of ads; upsell to a senior rep or the owner; sell 12-month instead of 3-month, or more touchpoints; downsell to a junior rep, shorter term, fewer calls, chat support instead of Zoom.

# Marketing
Qualified leads too expensive → with the back-end in LTV you can **raise your allowed CAC** and spend more on the niche message; move from leads self-scoring (friction) to **you scoring leads** by qualifications (who), behaviors (what they did), source (where from); route best leads to best closers; install attribution; start **CRO** with a regular split-test cadence (several 5–20% lifts across the funnel can double throughput).

- Split-test priority: **headline/subheadline** (cheap, high impact — ~30 tests on the ACQ homepage headline) → **the offer** (huge but expensive to change) → image → benefit bullets → proof → page order/above-the-fold placement.
- Goal: know **30-day cash collected** per customer. Break-even on acquisition within 30 days = scale ads hard; some ACQ companies happily lose money for 3–5 months because they know their numbers. You win by being able to outspend competitors.

# Sales
Reps set unrealistic expectations → refunds/bad reviews. Fix: (1) **sales aids** (slide decks, **VSLs**, sales letters, calculators, charts) — move the repeated education/belief-breaking part of the pitch before the call so calls are shorter and consistent; VSL structure = detailed pain → **proof, promise, plan** → why it hasn't been solved yet → cost of inaction → how the solution works/why it's better → proof throughout → name the risks openly and handle them → next step.
Goal: steady close rate (30% every week beats 20/40/20/40). (2) **Weekly game tape** across sales, CS, product, marketing.
(3) Track **NPS/CSAT/refund rate by sales rep** — refunds usually come from 1–2 reps who "sell hot" (over-promise). House rule: **state the facts and tell the truth; if the truth isn't compelling enough, change reality until it is.**

# Game tape — the 5 A's
(Leila's meeting):
- **Arrange** (head of sales books 60–90 min with heads of sales/product/marketing/CS
- Daily while there's a fire, weekly when stable) → **Assemble** (pull one recorded call — a loss or a great one
- Later onboarding/coaching calls too) → **Assess** (what does each department learn: marketing finds better hooks/pains, sales checks script/over-promising, CS spots promises it can't keep) → **Analyze** (one thing per department) → **Act** (commit to it within 7 days)

Makes you "a team of teams"; leaders are company leaders who happen to run a department.

- Portfolio case: consumer service business with no back-end → turned into SaaS, sales aids, more ad spend, tighter avatar, internal promotions → LTV doubled then +50% more; now $100M+runrate,valued~$350–600M.

# Customer service
Inconsistent answers → **CS playbook**: bucket all incoming questions into the 3–5 categories that cover most volume, write **templated answers** (like a sales script). **Empowerment wheel**: list what reps can do without approval (credits/refunds up to a limit, bonuses, minor ops decisions) vs what needs a manager (legal, major ops, regulatory).
Ritz-Carlton: up to $2k per guest per day. Gym Launch reps could give a free upgrade, free senior-coach time, or a custom gift up to $1k.

# Ascension path — 5 moments to offer the next product
(1) immediately (buying frenzy), (2) 24–48h later after first value, (3) **first big win** (testimonial, investment recouped — Gym Launch: when they'd made back the $16k), (4) halfway point (with qualifying indicators, e.g. netting enough per month), (5) last shot.
Tie each to a leading indicator. Upsells fail from wrong product, wrong time or wrong way — usually from not really trying. **Make it cool**: Gym Launch's last-shot mailer (zebra-print lumpy package, a $100 bill "dinner on me", rubber bands with a Pablo Escobar story, and a personal video in letter #2) for the $35–50k program.
Vary the hook each time you ask.

# IT
Company-owned hardware/software (don't skimp — $2–3k of gear pays back with one sale; work product and data belong to the company); dashboards and reporting.

# Recruiting
Avoid the **Peter Principle** (promoting people to their incompetence — you lose a great contributor and gain a bad manager).
Either run internal candidates through the full outside hiring process, or **"try before you buy"**:
- 60–90-day trial with milestones
- Grade the job description red/yellow/green and require all green. **Employee referrals**: referred hires stay ~70% longer
- Pay up to your cost-to-acquire-talent (agencies charge ~20% of salary)

ACQ went from $2k to $5k per referral. A friend's insurance agency paid $25k per productive agent (worth $250k/year) and it transformed the business.

# HR — firing well
Firing should never be a surprise — tell people where they stand (**red/yellow/green**) early and clearly; "if your friend doesn't know how bad it is, you're the problem". Plan coverage before the conversation (who takes what), time it to minimize disruption (end of day, before a team meeting, not before a big sales day), use a script, send a follow-up email (last paycheck, severance, benefits, equipment return).
Low-skill/low-will people usually weren't doing much anyway. Keeping someone with no future steals their future.

# Finance
Budget, save for big expenses/investments (events, bulk inventory, equipment, new locations), 6–12-month cash forecast, track write-offs.

lessons.t: Scaling 9 — Optimize (stage 6, 20–49 employees, role = LEADER; 77 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: everything is inefficient and workload keeps rising → grow by doing things better, not by doing more.**

~2.1M US companies. You now lead two layers (directors → managers → ICs) and must work through people.

# Product
Two products slow improvements → an **incremental improvement process for each product**: list every problem, estimate gain / cost / risk (and reach), re-rank, then **fix ONE at a time with everyone on it**. Saying "yes, that's a fire, and we're still not touching it" is the skill.
Magnifying-glass analogy: concentrate effort until you burn through, instead of warming the whole page. Leila's lesson for Alex: **missed opportunities ≠ problems** — solve existing problems before chasing new opportunities, or you scale both your problems and the new ones.
Leila's own lesson: chasing a 10/10 in every area creates competing priorities and makes everything mediocre; accept imperfection.

# Pruning
Ask customers "if we removed everything but one feature, which would you keep?" and "which one would make no difference if removed?" Then quietly delete the bottom one and watch. Skool found overwhelm is the #1 cancellation reason.
Gym Launch cut its 35-person tech-support team after it ranked last — churn and CSAT didn't move. If anyone complains, ask whether they're the customers you want to grow.
Community upvoting of features is "mid": customers can't imagine capabilities they don't know exist.

# Marketing — ad assembly process
To fight rising CAC from colder traffic: each week write **~50 hooks, 3–5 "meats", 1–3 CTAs** → 150–750 variations. The hook does ~80% of the work (Ogilvy: the headline spends 80 cents of your dollar), so spend ~80% of your time there.

- Hook sources in order of risk: your past ad winners → your content winners (a top Skool ad came from a content hook) → others' ad winners (steal from unrelated industries) → others' content winners → ad libraries (ads running 1–2+ months are winners; combine halves of hooks).
- Meat = the value-equation drivers and their mirror images (dream outcome vs nightmare, likelihood vs risk, speed vs delay, ease vs effort). Themes: product/service demo, testimonials/people, educational, narrative/emotional, non-human (memes, cartoons). **Sell the hole, not the drill** — Gym Launch's best ads showed a full gym, not leads.
- CTA: what to do, what they get, what happens next, and **show the next page/form in the ad** for congruence.
- "What limits your scaling is probably not your market but that your ads aren't good enough."

# Sales
Close rate on the core product drops/varies → **sales training system** (recorded best calls, perfect script with a **tone guide** — bold/italics/caps showing where to slow down, emphasize, ask with a question frame), **individual coaching** (role-play the rep's specific weakness: 2×/day week 1, daily week 2, weekly once productive; if not productive by end of week 2, strongly consider cutting), **sales-only game tape** where the rep presents their own mistakes first and teammates only say what went well, cadence = daily huddle + weekly team + weekly 1:1.
Managers must role-play too and be willing to look bad.

# Customer service
Churn rises → **segment churn by cohort** (sign-up month — what did you start/stop doing then?), by product, by sales rep and by CSM; look for the month churn spikes and intervene 1–2 months before it. Never fix churn by hiding the cancel button.

# 5 M's of activation
**Map** the journey (customer actions + your actions, colour-coded) → **Measure** patterns of your best customers (interview/focus group them) → **Make a hypothesis** about the true activation point (Gym Launch: owners who brought their operator/manager to the sales + onboarding calls nearly doubled retention) → **Monitor** with tests, changing only ONE thing at a time → **Modify** onboarding and even bake the activation behaviour into the offer/guarantee (a finance software gave 2 free months for attending 5 live training webinars; Alex used it ~4 years).

- Portfolio case: rebuilt webinar funnel, script and nurture → close rate 14.1% → 34.9%, ROAS 1.62 → 3.96, renewals 2% → 30%, profit margin 5% → 30%.

# IT
Cybersecurity — onboarding checklists, company email for every account, role-based security training (esp. anyone touching money), one-click offboarding.
Basics: firewall, encryption, MFA, patching, access control. Story: a spoofed vendor email diverted a $150k wire; cyber insurance covered it.

# Recruiting
Roles exceed your network → **become the headhunter** (LinkedIn Recruiter/InMail; short message with track record + "if not you, who do you know?" — two hires came via referrals from people who said no). **Four-person four-way fit** for senior roles: recruiter screens expectations, two leaders interview culture and skill, founder interviews potential.
Founder involved in all management hires. 4–5 references for senior people, 30–45 min each, same questions, **two follow-ups per answer**.
Senior candidates negotiate — it's normal; several comp calls; talk money openly from day one.

# HR
Benefits + retirement + advanced comp to attract senior talent. Benefits often return more than cash comp (people value them above cost); budget ~15–30% of payroll.
Choose providers on needs, industry fit, reputation, usable tech, admin support; **sell** the benefits to the team; re-quote annually.
Advanced comp "5 S's":
- **set** strategic goals (attract vs retain
- Performance vs market-based
- Tie to 1–2 metrics the person most controls) → **segment** pay (base + bonus + benefits as one package
- At this size lead with performance upside) → **study** market benchmarks → **set** performance metrics tied to career path → **start, share, simplify** with a template per level (e.g. managers up to 25% bonus, directors up to 75%)

Only add complexity if you can't attract or keep talent.

# Finance
Spending to grow but not growing → **FinOps**:
- Gross margin and LTV:CAC **by product line, traffic source, customer set**
- Financial dashboard showing each department's cost and return (can you explain how every department makes money?)
- Balance sheet for assets (equipment, IP, domains)
- Quarterly taxes
- Scale AR (collections pays for itself
- Put it near CS so it's empathetic — "did you switch cards?") and AP (be every vendor's best customer)

Insurance: cyber + business interruption. Shift from **deciding by intuition to deciding by information**.

lessons.t: Scaling 10 — Categorize (stage 7, 50–99 employees, role = EXECUTIVE; 72 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: every system is overwhelmed and the business is disorganized → triage and put everything into buckets.**

~1.2M US companies (≈3–4% of businesses). Structure: ICs → managers → directors → a partial executive team (Gym Launch's first exec was a CFO, chosen to cover the founders' weakest area).
The founder becomes the CEO, formally or not.

# Product
Product ages, improvements roll out too slowly → **one problem, one team, one measurable objective** — pick the problem with the biggest reward, not the easiest. GitHub founder story: whole engineering team on the single top complaint until solved, then the next.
"Concurrent thinking" is a fallacy — context switching makes 5 parallel things take ~5× longer. With more people you don't do more things at once; you do **one bigger thing**.
Protect the team's attention (shower time, dinner conversation), not just hours. "Companies die from the inside out" and "of indigestion, not starvation." Leaving the rest of the business alone often improves it — every change carries a guaranteed cost, only a possible upside.
Example: a portfolio company's only priority for 18–24 months = converting from service to SaaS.

# Marketing
One channel makes lead flow volatile (often at ~$1–2M/month) → fund a **second acquisition channel**, padded by cash from **referrals** and **segmented nurture**. Expect ~**12 months** to payback: months of spend-10/lose-10 before it flips; track progress step by step (clicks → opt-ins → bookings → shows).
Gym Launch's outbound took 3 months for a first sale; at month 6 the exec team staged an "intervention"; Alex persisted because he could see funnel-stage progress; it reached ~50% of revenue after a year.

- Put a **0→1 builder** on new initiatives, not a 5→10 optimizer. Rule: **don't put a new person on a new thing, and don't put one person on two initiatives** (backfill your best operator first, then move them).

# 7 referral plays
(from $100M Leads):
- One-sided referral paying ~your CAC
- **two-sided** (split it — friend gets a discount, referrer gets a reward
- Better relational optics)
- Simply **ask on the sales call "want to bring someone?"** (one rep doubled sales this way)
- Trade discounts for referrals
- Quarterly **referral events** ("bring a friend")
- Referral promo days (e.g. double bonus Fridays)
- Unlockable status-based referral bonuses

# Segmented nurture
Segment email by lead score (who, what they did, source) — HubSpot-cited lift of several hundred percent; email ROI often quoted ~36–45:1.

- Second-channel order of risk: same platform/placement + **new audience** → same platform/audience + **new placement** → **new platform** in the same Core-Four bucket (e.g. Meta feed → YouTube pre-roll) → finally a **new Core-Four activity** (riskiest — what Gym Launch did with outbound).

# Sales
Leads wasted → better **schedule coverage** (7 days, long hours, 15-min slots; never fake "busy" bookings), setter 3% incentive, automated + clearly-human manual reminders (company iPhones for blue bubbles), **three-way intro text** setter → closer → prospect, daily kudos for show rate, show-up bribe (kickboxing gym: "pink or black gloves?"), **local area codes**.
New reps get the worst shifts (weekends); top closer picks schedule. Match hours to the customer's availability (gym owners are free midday).

# Customer service
Purely reactive → proactive **customer journey with a lane for each of the 4 R's** — Retain, Review (feedback from haters, reviews from fans), Refer, Resell — plus customer vs employee lanes. Triggers in the CRM: **time-based, behavior-based, event-based**.
Fix retain + review first so referrals/ascension become obvious. Split CS into reactive and proactive teams.
Case: a stalled company simplified its product mess into a simple **A/B offer** → faster rep onboarding, less customer overwhelm, simpler delivery → higher margin; PE offer within 18 months.

# IT
Centralize data in the cloud with backups (AWS saved them when a custom-tool vendor went bust), central hardware custody, naming/folder conventions ("local cost, global benefit").

# Recruiting
An **ATS** (easy UX above all, integrations, AI parsing/scheduling/matching, funnel analytics: resumes → screen → interview pass rates, scalable) + **specialized recruiting firms** for recurring, non-company-specific roles. Vet recruiters by placement success rate (best ≈100%), references, and **speed** — how fast they respond to you is how fast they'll work candidates (top candidates are gone in ~9 days).
Trial them on one low-stakes role.

# HR
An **HRIS** (records, payroll/benefits, time & attendance, onboarding, **performance management**/engagement dashboards). Choose for growth headroom (don't be a vendor's biggest client), integrations, stakeholder input (not committee), trials; negotiate (you're now an enterprise buyer).
Cultures collapse at 50–100 because they're accidental — **operationalize what's working**.

# Finance
Team spends money badly → spending SOP (who can spend up to what, on which categories; above that, an approval process), **department budgets** built from observed spend then pruned, cards with per-person limits (custom card program, points on big categories), marketing unlimited as long as it's within profitability KPIs, real 12-month operating projections so leaders can invest (many under-spend), more insurance as exposure grows.
Managing expenses and focus are permanent jobs, never "solved".

lessons.t: Scaling 11 — Specialize (stage 8, 100–249 employees, role = PRESIDENT; 58 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: nobody can know everything and focus is too broad → dedicated people and teams for specific tasks.**

~900k US companies. Four layers (execs, directors, managers, leads).
You now lead a community / "team of teams".

# Product
Too many features overwhelm customers → **survey, prune, improve through deletion**; pruned features can become paid cross-sells/add-ons. Customers usually say "it's worth it just for X" — the rest dilutes value.
Aim for "magical" products that deliver with near-zero customer effort (alarm systems, Wi-Fi). McKinsey: top-decile CEOs prune ~6× more and are far more profitable; uncontrolled growth behaves like cancer.
Musk: keep deleting until you have to add ~10% back. Dragon Dictation v2: zero new features, just better accuracy.
Think **"value per second, not seconds of value"** (density).

- Value map: **trash** (low value, low willingness to pay) · **table stakes** (high value, everyone does it — low pricing power) · **differentiators** (high value only you deliver — pricing power) · **niche value** (high for some → carve into add-ons). Look to customers, not competitors.

# Marketing
Broad creative attracts worse leads and dilutes the brand → grow the brand with **standardized messaging** (own 1–3 words in people's minds:
- For Alex "acquisition / business / value"
- Colours/fonts only exist to reinforce the association), a **simple mission**, **big free value** (B2B: real monetary value — books, courses, tools, calculators, white papers like McKinsey/Bain, free low-level service
- Aim for "you've paid for yourself 100× before I bought anything"

B2C: entertainment and pairing with entertainers who share your values), and **big positive associations** (endorsements, sponsorships). Repetition is the job — "100 ways to say one thing, not one way to say 100 things" (Nike's "Just Do It").

# Sales
Superstars get drowned out by average reps → **route the best leads to the best closers** (front end and ascension sales), automated metrics per rep/platform/product, assignment rules. Contacting leads within 60 seconds can multiply revenue — only possible when top closers get only top leads.
Story:
- The #1 timeshare rep (of ~3,000) asked the CEO for the best-credit leads
- Tested at one location → 5× productivity
- Rolled out → company went from ~$200–250M to $1.2B in ~3 years

Juniors sharpen their teeth on weaker leads; top closers' earnings attract talent (survivorship-bias motivation).

# Customer service
Multiple product journeys conflict/poorly timed → a **blended customer journey** mapping every path (A→B, B→A, A+B…), tag customers by path, separate onboarding/email/CS per path, and **cut low-LTV, high-effort paths** to free resources. Gym Launch → Prestige Labs path had far higher LTV than the reverse (same CAC); selling both together didn't work.
Customers who skipped the front-end product straight into the back end churned early — premium-direct entry needs its own marketing, sales team and onboarding (they eventually built a separate product line to do it).

# IT
Departments outgrow general software → specialized stacks per department, **decentralized IT** (MarTech, sales ops, CS ops, RevOps, FinOps), ticketing + **SLAs** per function. Caution: internal tools are a competitive moat, not a SaaS business to spin off — buyers won't value a solar sales company as SaaS.

# Recruiting
Recruiters drift on standards → **standardized selection**: structured interviews (same 5–10 questions per interview type per role), **interview panels** including people from other departments who have no urgency to fill the seat, a **founder final check** (~20 min; Leila stacks 5–6 in one morning a week and watches prior interview recordings to probe the biggest red flag), and a **simple scoring rubric** (1–5 on the role's top 5 skills + each core value).
Likability and interviewing skill ≠ job ability; some of their best hires interviewed terribly.

# HR
Performance suffers, complaints rise → group onboarding software, a **performance-management system** (1:1 notes, weekly upward feedback on managers, CEO surveys, red/yellow/green goal tracking per department), **reinforce values constantly** (twice-monthly leadership/team training; weekly shout-outs tied to core values; Gym Launch mailed a t-shirt printed with the value someone exemplified).
Hiring/firing/promoting decisions communicate values more than words. EPLI insurance.

# Finance
Still paying retail, cash idle → quarterly subscription purge (someone assertive must push deletions; Twitter cut ~80% of staff and kept running), **re-shop every vendor** with competing quotes for enterprise pricing and better service tiers, put cash in **yield accounts** (5% on $10M = $500k), **internal audits** (most theft is internal), specialized tax roles (R&D credits etc.), founder reviews the P&L line by line monthly with written variance notes.
The best CFOs are cheap and ruthless — a yin to the founder's yang. "It's not what you make, it's what you keep."

lessons.t: Scaling 12 — Capitalize (stage 9, 250–500 employees, role = CHAIRMAN; 52 min)
lessons.md:
> **Bottom line: growth plateaus and you're unsure where the next leg comes from → make a big bet on the future.**

~300k US companies. Structure: division leaders running mini-companies (each with its own marketing, sales, CS).
Keep as few layers as possible.

# Product — buy or build the next "rising star"
Changing the cash cow now tends to hurt it (long-time customers want it left alone). BCG matrix: **stars** (growing market, growing share), **cash cows** (high share, slow market), **question marks** (bets), **dogs** (low share, no growth).
Act like an investor: read market trends (tech adoption, what customers will ask for next, underserved geographies like LatAm). A portfolio company bet on an AI-driven product ~16 months early as AI was wiping out small competitors — now succeeding.
Optimize for risk-adjusted return (reach, impact, confidence, expense).

# Buy
When speed matters and it's not core, for licences/regulatory assets, for cost savings/cross-sell, or to become a platform roll-up (Waste Management). Know what you're buying: customers, team, product, list.
A friend buys retiring wealth managers' books — cheaper than CAC × 500 clients one by one. Best leading indicator of cross-sell: customers already overlap.
You can also buy a specialist vendor (e.g. a TikTok agency) instead of building the team.

# Build
When it's core to your future (better long-term outcomes, same culture); hire whole teams from competitors with big signing bonuses (acqui-hire).

# Marketing
Attribution breaks across channels, compliance becomes a risk → **brand-first, omnichannel, blended ROAS**, plus a **compliance process** (the biggest risk is still going out of business from not advertising; rules: state the facts, tell the truth, substantiate claims, refund when asked; legal-built checklist signed off before anything ships; distinguish platform risk from regulatory risk).

# New Balance
After ~15 years of decline a new CMO flipped spend from 70/30 direct-response to 70/30 brand (collabs, endorsements, awareness). Sales fell for ~18 more months, then surged.
Lessons:
- Brand takes ~18 months to pay
- ~**3–4 parts give : 1 part ask** (TV, YouTube and feeds run ~3 content : 1 ad
- TikTok ran no ads for years to grow)

- Judge direct-response ROAS **blended** with brand spend (a "21:1" funnel might really be 4–5:1). New CEOs can look brilliant for a year by draining the goodwill bank — keep "digging the well before you're thirsty". Founders win by thinking longer-term than hired managers.
- Advanced math: **cost to acquire a permanent customer** (e.g. if 1 in 3 trials converts and 1 in 3 customers survives past the churn cliff, a permanent customer costs ~9 trials) → shows exactly how much cash to push through to reach $1B+.

# Sales
Too many leads/products for one rep → reps specialize by **product, lead type, process and territory** (e.g. nano-influencer vs mega-influencer vs wholesale teams, each with its own pipeline, comp, training).
Specialization shortens training. Match reps to regions culturally.
Processes vary: 1-call close → 2 calls with a sales aid → 5+ calls with multiple stakeholders.

# Customer service
Volume breaks support → **triage** routing to specialized reps by product/tier, which creates a **career ladder** for reps (lower tier → product 2 → enterprise, with raises — extends the LTV of your talent); standardized notes so customers never repeat themselves; channel-based routing rules; CS per division.

# IT
Old stack breaks → updated segmented stacks per division, enterprise software (ERP like NetSuite), a "czar" per function, triage/SLAs so IT isn't treated as free help, in-house developers.

# Recruiting
Top talent only answers the founder → **founder as chief recruiter for rainmakers** (people with rolodexes, distribution, whole teams). Courting can take 6–18 months (Jobs cited 12–18 months for top people; Zuckerberg had regular dinners with Sheryl Sandberg for about a year).
"Beyond a certain level no one works for you — they work with you." Landing one such person can be worth more than a $10–20M contract.

# HR — strategic workforce planning
(org design): from company objectives, plan who/how many/how fast, promotions, backfills for expected churn (at 250+ people even 5% monthly churn = 12–25 people/month), redundancies, hyper-specialization; a 12–18-month workforce plan. Leila's colour-coded org map: green (promote internally), yellow (someone there but weak), red (missing leader).
Managers rate their people red/yellow/green. **RACI** per team (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) to expose overloaded or under-used people.

# Finance — "prep for sale"
(not necessarily to sell): quality of earnings, ask investment bankers what's wrong with your business (free consulting from an investor's/lender's eye), clean house, third-party audits (a friend found an employee had stolen $20M+), fix legal/capital structure, hedge big commodity inputs (Ray Dalio/McDonald's example), open access to debt and strategic partners (e.g. sell 10% to a partner who brings 10,000-store distribution).
Like fixing up a house to sell and deciding to keep it.

- Beyond 500 people: Alex and Leila say they haven't been there yet, so they don't teach it.

Alex asks people who got results from the courses/content to submit their story via the form on the site; each month some are featured and one random submitter is invited to Acquisition.com HQ in Las Vegas. (Same bonus video appears at the end of the Offers course.)

videos.md:
## Starting a Business & Choosing a Vehicle

189 ideas from 106 videos. [#N] = video N in the Start here tab.

- Stages of change: uninformed optimism, informed pessimism, crisis of meaning (valley of despair), informed optimism, success. Most people quit at the valley and restart something new at stage one, and each restart in business costs years, not seconds. [▶ 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RdAKXJlMIZM)
- Focus beats diversification for small businesses: pick one thing and go all in. Example of a roofer also doing contracting and flipping; the money "left on the table" is really the focus he isn't giving to the core business. Top self-made fortunes come from boring single industries held for decades. [▶ 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RdAKXJlMIZM)
- "Magic wand" exercise: imagine every side project except the best one vanished; usually growing the remaining one becomes obvious, and what blocks you is a few hard conversations (firing, shutting down, ending partnerships). [▶ 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RdAKXJlMIZM)
- Focus instead of diversifying early: your scarce resource is time and attention, so pour it into one opportunity until it overflows; wealthy people diversify only after one stream made them rich. The question is not which idea will work but which one you will actually work on. [▶ 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBoRLJimVzc)
- Pick a hungry crowd: market matters more than offer, which matters more than persuasion skill. A good market has four traits: acute pain, purchasing power, easy to target, and growing; you need all four. [▶ 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBoRLJimVzc)
- Increase income first through jobs that need no experience: remote phone-sales starter roles (around $40k+/year), or driving Uber in spare hours. Buy a $5-10k car in cash to avoid payments. [▶ 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YFA8AS5Cu2w)
- Enter a new job and double the inputs of the hardest worker (twice the doors or dials), then give it about 36 months: be patient with outputs, impatient with inputs. When you feel things should be faster, use action as the coping mechanism. [▶ 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aFoMYz_jWcs)
- Avoid opportunity hopping: most people cycle uninformed optimism, informed pessimism and the valley of despair, then jump to a new thing. Push through to informed optimism and success; downturns reward those who stay, because market share shifts to the few left standing. [▶ 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MNll1BaskLA)
- Which vehicle you pick matters more than effort (Buffett's classmate who went into steel versus Buffett's partnership). Small and big goals take similar effort, and top talent only joins big opportunities, so aim big. [▶ 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qxQIcDrre1E)
- Pick a starving crowd: pain, purchasing power, easy to target, growing. Choose the avatar you can help most and productize for low operational drag. Five ways to expand a market: go upmarket, downmarket, adjacent, broader, or deeper (his favorite: more ad spend, outbound, new platforms, buying competitors). [▶ 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qxQIcDrre1E)
- Treat real estate or any field as active income you learn deeply, not passive income; people who get rich in it spend huge time finding and walking deals. [▶ 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dZ7xeVCYC5M)
- Keeping personal risk near zero lets you take more business shots: his savings from a consulting job funded the first gym, and low living costs let him recover after losing everything twice (nine failed businesses, seven failed partnerships). [▶ 12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymFWgFiKUvM)
- "Three Ps" for picking what to sell: a Pain you personally overcame (a mother of nine's system for packing lunches), your Profession (a dietitian who now teaches other dietitians to bill insurance, earning close to $1M/year with about 5,800 followers), or a Passion you consume constantly (his fitness obsession led to a gym). Any job skill can become consulting, contracting or teaching others in that field. [▶ 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nIk3DedjxJM)
- Do not wait for the perfect pick; choose your "best bad idea" quickly so customer feedback can make it less wrong over time. [▶ 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nIk3DedjxJM)
- Pick who to serve from three groups: people like you (his recommendation, since you already know their pains and you become a mission-driven founder), people you have helped before (his first $100 came from unsolicited nutrition advice at a pizza shop), or underserved growing markets. [▶ 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nIk3DedjxJM)
- "Follow your passion" breaks down in specifics: he left consulting for fitness, but running a gym meant training weight-loss clients repetitively, not elite athletes. Building any business around a passion means mostly doing unrelated work (sourcing, logistics, sales, taxes, influencer outreach). [▶ 15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UDBkiBnMrHs)
- Be irreplaceable: if a standard degree qualifies anyone for your job, you will be paid what everyone else accepts. Do what most people are not doing, and assume you might be wrong so you keep learning from everyone. [▶ 19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ySuYdJ0H4s)
- Ramsey Solutions started primitively: Ramsey volunteered on a bankrupt Nashville talk station, self-published a book from his living room in 1992, and launched a money class in 1994 where three of the first four attendees bought; it became Financial Peace University (about 10 million participants via some 50,000 churches) and the company now earns a little over $300M/year. [▶ 21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jvXOOddDg_s)
- Roughly 90% of businesses never reach $1M/yr, about 9% pass it, and only around 0.4% (1 in 250) reach $10M+. Getting there depends on two things: how skilled the entrepreneur is and how much leverage the vehicle (business model) gives them. [▶ 22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nh8Oc7ERdIU)
- Same skills, better vehicle: he moved from owning gyms, to a done-for-you gym turnaround service, to licensing his playbook, and each jump multiplied results. A portfolio company went from an agency to owning all of its photography studios and reached about $2.5M/month across 30+ locations in about 30 months. A mentor told him he had a top-tier skill set stuck in a low-tier opportunity. [▶ 22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nh8Oc7ERdIU)
- Time in one vehicle is leverage too. Every switch resets you to zero, so the new vehicle has to be far better. Panda Express (about $3.7B in sales, around 27% margins, fully owned) shows what 45 years in one business can compound into. If you have years of industry experience, prefer a half-pivot within the same industry over starting fresh somewhere else. [▶ 22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nh8Oc7ERdIU)
- How to transition: take jobs where you get paid to learn, even at a big pay cut (he went from consulting to $14/hr personal training), and tell your employer what you want to learn. Then live below your means, stack cash, and grow a side hustle until it matches your salary. Keep that up for about 6 months before quitting so one good month doesn't fool you.
